notes.meaning: King Abijah died and was buried with the earlier kings in Jerusalem. His son Asa became the new king, and God granted the land ten years of peace. This quiet period came partly because the northern kingdom of Israel was still weak from its earlier defeat.

Asa chose to live and govern in a way that pleased God rather than pleasing himself or the world. He made it his aim to follow God's commands faithfully. While he was not perfect, his main goal was to do what God called good and right.

Asa began a nationwide cleanup by tearing down altars built for foreign gods. He smashed the stone pillars used in pagan worship and chopped down the wooden poles set up for the false goddess Asherah. He removed these objects so the people would not be tempted into idol worship.

Asa did not stop at destroying idols; he commanded the people of Judah to turn back to the Lord. He called on them to pray, worship God alone, and obey His laws. He used his royal authority and personal example to lead the nation back to faithful living.

Asa cleared away the shrines and sun-worship altars from every town across Judah. Because the people turned away from false worship, God blessed the kingdom with peace and safety. True quietness and rest followed the return to God's ways.

Asa took advantage of the peaceful years to strengthen and protect the cities of Judah. He knew this rest was a gift from the Lord, so he used the time wisely instead of becoming lazy. Preparing defenses during peacetime was a sign of practical wisdom.

Asa told the leaders to surround their towns with walls, towers, and strong gates while no enemies were attacking. He reminded them that God had given them this peace and security because they had sought Him. The people united behind his plan, and their building projects succeeded.

Asa organized a large army of brave men from the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. The men of Judah carried heavy spears and large body shields for close-up fighting, while the men of Benjamin used bows and smaller shields for long-distance combat. Both groups brought different fighting skills that served the whole nation well.

A huge army of one million soldiers and three hundred chariots marched up from the south under a commander named Zerah. This invading force advanced as far as the Judean town of Mareshah. The sudden threat tested Judah's faith, since the enemy vastly outnumbered Asa's troops.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Zerah was a Nubian general in the Egyptian army under Pharaoh Osorkon I, and that the phrase 'a thousand thousand' was an ancient way of describing a countless multitude rather than an exact census.

notes.meaning: Asa did not wait in fear behind city walls; he marched out to the southern border to meet the invaders. He placed his soldiers in battle lines across the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah. This open valley gave his smaller army room to make an organized stand.

Before joining battle, Asa cried out to God in wholehearted prayer. He declared that numbers do not matter to the Lord, who can easily save the weak from the mighty. Asa asked God to step in and defend His own honor against frail, mortal enemies.

differ.view: Preachers emphasize Asa's prayer as a supreme example of resting entirely in God's power, while noting that strong faith in one crisis does not guarantee one will avoid unbelief in future trials.
Teachers highlight Asa's prayer as a model for spiritual warfare, showing how turning over impossible battles to God releases His supernatural intervention.

notes.meaning: The Lord answered Asa's cry and threw the Cushite army into panic and confusion. The invaders could not stand their ground and ran away in full retreat before Judah. Scripture gives the entire credit for this sudden turnaround to the Lord Himself.

Asa and his soldiers chased the fleeing enemy more than twenty miles toward the city of Gerar. The Cushites were completely broken before the Lord and His army, leaving them unable to rally or fight back. After the rout, the men of Judah collected huge amounts of leftover goods and armor.

Judah's troops went on to defeat the towns surrounding Gerar that had allied with the invading army. A deep fear sent by the Lord fell upon those cities, leaving them powerless to resist. Asa's men took large amounts of stored goods from each place.

The soldiers also took over the nomadic camps that supplied the enemy with pack animals and food. They captured great herds of sheep and camels before heading home. The victorious army then returned to Jerusalem, enriched and safeguarded by God's rescue.
